_meta.purpose: Plants we might bring back to Fernwood. Distinct from plants.json — that file tracks what is on the property; this file tracks what could be. Per the depth filter, every candidate has to fit Fernwood's actual reality: 2,873 ft Blue Ridge, zone 6b, Cove Forest + Low-to-Mid Elevation Oak Forest mosaic with potential Seepage Wetlands in the spring drainage.
_meta.communityReference: Natural Communities of Blue Ridge Ecoregion (GNPS, adapted from Edwards, Ambrose, Kirkman 2013 UGA Press)

categories.restoration: Multi-decade canopy / regional restoration species. Slow, relational (TACF, HRI). Most ecologically meaningful.
categories.keystone: Tallamy-defined keystone genera for Blue Ridge ecoregion — species that support disproportionate caterpillar / Lepidoptera diversity (oaks 400+, cherries 450+, willows 380+).
categories.rich-cove: Special-concern flora of the rich cove community. Look-don't-pick if found on the property; if planting, only ethical-propagation sources.
categories.cultivar-trial: Native genus with a published Mt. Cuba Center trial; the trial winner is the defensible cultivar pick.
categories.bird-pollinator: Strong wildlife value — Audubon Plants for Birds + Xerces Southeast pollinator list + NWF Native Plant Finder zip 30143.
categories.native-grass: Native bunchgrasses and graminoids for understory, forest edge, or seepage zones.
categories.turf: Grasses and lawn alternatives for the managed fairway turf — the practical tall fescue alongside lower-input and native-leaning options worth trialing as the lawn leans toward the natural approach.

candidates.name: Autumn bentgrass
candidates.rationale: A native perennial bunchgrass that takes partial shade and mesic-to-wet soils — the kind of grass that would belong in the spring drainage and along the mesic forest edges.
candidates.notes: Bunchgrass habit — no rhizomes, no stolons — gentle in a planted setting. Eight to thirty-one inches tall, with airy late-season inflorescences.
candidates.curationNotes: Not in the GNPS Blue Ridge landscaping matrix, but iNaturalist + Native Plant Trust + Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center all confirm the habitat (mesic to dry forests, seepage swamps, depressions) matches the property.

candidates.name: American chestnut
candidates.rationale: Once a dominant canopy species at this elevation in the southern Appalachians. The blight (introduced 1904) killed virtually all mature trees from Maine to Georgia by 1950. One of the two big landowner-participation restoration species. This slope was once chestnut canopy.
candidates.notes: This is a multi-year commitment, not a sale-stand purchase. TACF GA's own framing: "Many trees today may not carry sufficient disease resistance, so most likely will not live to become the 'mighty giants' we all hope and dream about." Path is national membership → Potential Orchard Steward form → stewardship plan with GA Science Coordinator → germplasm agreement. They recommend a few years of membership + volunteering before planting. Smaller path: pure American chestnut seedlings at the annual spring sale. Most ecologically meaningful candidate on this list; also the slowest and least guaranteed.

attribution.author: The original uploader was Peatcher at German Wikipedia.

candidates.name: Eastern hemlock
candidates.rationale: Cool-drainage native, occurs in acidic Cove Forest sites. Likely already present on the property in the spring drainage. Threatened by Hemlock Woolly Adelgid (HWA) since 2003 in Georgia; statewide by 2012. No other native conifer fills hemlock's ecological role.
candidates.notes: ACTIONABLE NOW: check existing hemlocks on the property for HWA and treat (imidacloprid + dinotefuran soil drench at root flare). HRI has DIY landowner instructions. FUTURE / NOT YET AVAILABLE: resistant-stock plantings for forest restoration — HRI's genetic-resistance work is still early-stage and there is no current sourcing pathway for landowners. Two ornamental landscape cultivars ('Traveler', 'Crossroads') are expected to be released for purchase "in the near future" but are explicitly landscape-only, not forest restoration stock. Step 1 is the only step worth taking this year.

candidates.name: Flame azalea
candidates.rationale: Signature North Georgia mountain native — the Cohutta and Smokies range is centered on this species. Brilliant May-June bloom. Confirmed in GNPS Blue Ridge landscaping list for both Montane Oak and Cove Forest understory.
candidates.notes: If sourcing from Gardens of the Blue Ridge: they specialize in native azaleas including hard-to-find color forms. Drainage matters — happiest on sloped, well-drained, acidic soil.

candidates.name: White oak
candidates.rationale: The keystone genus per Tallamy. Each oak supports 400+ Lepidoptera species — the foundation for nearly every songbird's nesting season. Confirmed in Low-to-Mid Elevation Oak Forest community at this elevation.
candidates.notes: GFC seedling sale typically offers multiple oak species at landowner-scale quantities and prices. December-March planting. If choosing one keystone tree to plant first, this is the answer.

candidates.name: Smooth (wild) hydrangea
candidates.rationale: A native of the cove forests at this elevation — the wild cousin to the hydrangeas already by the porch. The 'Haas' Halo' selection is the defensible pick: Mt. Cuba Center's 2022 trial named it the strongest in the Mid-Atlantic.
candidates.notes: The existing plants.json hydrangea entries are mixed natives + Hydrangea macrophylla (non-native). Adding 'Haas' Halo' is a clean way to deepen the native component without removing what's planted. Mt. Cuba's full trial report: mtcubacenter.org/trials/hydrangea/

candidates.name: 'Claire Grace' wild bergamot
candidates.rationale: Wild bergamot is native to the north Georgia mountains and would fit a sunny edge of the fairway. 'Claire Grace' is the defensible cultivar — Mt. Cuba's 40-selection trial named it the clear winner: three-week floral display, 130+ butterfly and moth visits over the trial, strong powdery-mildew resistance.
candidates.notes: Pollinator workhorse for a sunny-to-part-shade bed. Pairs naturally with cardinal flower for a hummingbird + butterfly combination. Mt. Cuba report: mtcubacenter.org/trials/monarda/

candidates.name: 'Screamin' Yellow' yellow wild indigo
candidates.rationale: A long-lived perennial with a deep taproot, drought-tolerant once established — would suit a full-sun bed at the fairway edge or a patio corner. 'Screamin' Yellow' is the trial-tested cultivar pick: Mt. Cuba's baptisia trial (46 selections, 2012-2015) named it the top performer. Bright yellow spring spikes.
candidates.notes: Worth flagging — B. sphaerocarpa is a south-central species, not a Blue Ridge native. For a more local fit, the same Mt. Cuba trial's 'Purple Smoke' (a hybrid involving B. australis, which IS native to the southern Appalachians) does the same garden work. Either way: full sun, well-drained — not for the forest interior.

candidates.name: 'Pica Bella' purple coneflower
candidates.rationale: Purple coneflower is native to woodland edges and open glades across the eastern US, north Georgia included — a fit for a sunny edge along the fairway or patio bed. 'Pica Bella' is the defensible cultivar: Mt. Cuba's 75-selection trial (2018-2020) named it the top performer; 'Fragrant Angel' averaged the most butterfly visits.
candidates.notes: 12 cultivars rated outstanding (4.3+/5) — defensible alternatives if 'Pica Bella' isn't available. Avoid the heavily-bred doubles and orange/yellow color novelties; Mt. Cuba's trial showed they underperform on both vigor and pollinator visits. Mt. Cuba report: mtcubacenter.org/trials/echinacea-mid-atlantic-region/

candidates.name: 'Summer Sunshine' swamp coreopsis
candidates.rationale: A wet-meadow native that would suit the pond's edge or the spring drainage seepage. 'Summer Sunshine' is the trial-tested pick: Mt. Cuba's coreopsis trial (94 selections) named it the top performer for disease-resistant foliage and late-season bloom.
candidates.notes: Worth flagging — C. palustris is a coastal-plain wetland species, not a Blue Ridge native. The pond and spring drainage could host it if the trial winner is the priority. For a Blue Ridge native alternative, 'Zagreb' threadleaf coreopsis (C. verticillata 'Zagreb') was also a top performer in the same trial — and a better fit for dry sunny spots than for the pond's edge.

candidates.name: Pink lady's slipper
candidates.rationale: Native orchid; rich-cove special-concern species. Confirmed in GNPS Blue Ridge Cove Forest list. If found on the property, leave alone and support — do not transplant. If planting, only from ethical-propagation sources (never wild-collected).
candidates.notes: Mycorrhizal-dependent — moves poorly. ABG Safeguarding Nursery is the propagation partner for any rare-species restoration thread. Worth walking the north-facing slopes in May to look for the existing colony before considering sourcing.

candidates.name: Cardinal flower
candidates.rationale: Pond-edge and seepage native; the strongest hummingbird-attractor in eastern North America. Confirmed in GNPS Blue Ridge Seepage Wetland list. Direct fit for the pond area and the spring drainage.
candidates.notes: Short-lived perennial but self-sows freely in suitable conditions. Pair with great blue lobelia (Lobelia siphilitica) for blue + red pollinator bed.

candidates.name: Christmas fern
candidates.rationale: Year-round evergreen native fern — confirmed in GNPS Blue Ridge Low-to-Mid Oak Forest list. Excellent winter texture in the woodland understory; hosts insects that overwinter and feed early-spring birds.
candidates.notes: One of the easiest natives to establish under existing tree canopy. UGA Extension B 987-2 (Ferns) is the deep reference.

candidates.name: Common witchhazel
candidates.rationale: Native understory shrub / small tree. Yellow-strap-petaled flowers in October-November when virtually nothing else is blooming — important late-season pollinator resource. Confirmed in GNPS Blue Ridge list across Cove, Low-Mid Oak, and Seepage communities.
candidates.notes: Distinct from the spring-blooming Asian witch hazels common in nursery trade. The late-season bloom is the diagnostic feature. Slow to establish but very long-lived.

candidates.name: Little bluestem
candidates.rationale: The signature warm-season bunchgrass of southern Appalachian uplands — blue-green through summer, copper-red after frost. The backbone of the fairway-fringe meadow on dry, sunny ground.
candidates.notes: Host plant for several skipper butterflies and a seed source for sparrows. Tough, drought-tolerant, and clump-forming — it won't run. Sow a regionally-adapted (eastern) ecotype, not generic Midwest stock.

candidates.name: Big bluestem
candidates.rationale: The tall companion to little bluestem — four to six feet, with the forked “turkeyfoot” seedhead. Adds height and structure to the meadow on deeper, moister ground.
candidates.notes: Native across Georgia. Best where the soil holds a little more moisture than little bluestem prefers — the lower fairway fringe toward the spring drainage.

candidates.name: Indiangrass
candidates.rationale: Golden, plume-headed warm-season native that completes the classic bluestem–indiangrass meadow trio. Tall, upright, and luminous in low autumn light.
candidates.notes: Pairs naturally with the bluestems and the meadow wildflowers. Warm-season — greens late and holds gold structure through winter until the late-February cut.

candidates.name: Switchgrass
candidates.rationale: The most adaptable of the warm-season natives — takes everything from dry to seasonally wet, which suits the damp lower edge of the fairway fringe toward the spring drainage.
candidates.notes: Roundstone offers a Georgia-ecotype switchgrass — the right provenance for this slope. Good cover and seed for birds; airy panicles catch the light.

candidates.name: Purpletop
candidates.rationale: The native grass that already shows up on its own in unmowed North Georgia fairway edges and old fields — purple-tinged seedheads in late summer. Recognizing it is half the meadow work.
candidates.notes: Often arrives without planting once the mowing eases off, so the first move in the fringe may simply be to stop mowing and see what's already there. Larval host for several skippers. Sometimes called grease grass for the sheen on its seedheads.

candidates.name: Turf-type tall fescue
candidates.rationale: The grass already running the fairway, listed here for the choice that matters when overseeding: a quality turf-type blend, not old pasture-grade “Kentucky 31.” UGA's standard cool-season lawn grass for the North Georgia mountains.
candidates.notes: Non-native (Eurasian) — the one practical exception to the native-first thinking on this list, earned by being the realistic choice for a lush mowed turf at this elevation. Turf-type blends are darker, finer, denser, and more shade- and heat-tolerant than Kentucky 31. Sold as seed at local feed-and-seed and garden centers; overseed thin spots every September.
candidates.curationNotes: Kept honest: tracked in plants.json as the Fairway Turf the property already grows. It lives here in Candidates only for the cultivar / seed decision when refreshing the stand.

candidates.name: Fine-fescue no-mow blend
candidates.rationale: The lower-input bridge between manicured turf and meadow — a blend of fine fescues (creeping red, chewings, hard, sheep) that grows soft, fine, and low, asking far less mowing, water, and fertilizer than tall fescue.
communityFit: Low-input lawn — sun to part shade
candidates.notes: Fine fescues struggle in the hot, humid Piedmont but are far more viable up here, where summers run 10–15°F cooler. Worth trialing on a turf area you're willing to let read softer and looser than the main fairway — mow occasionally to ~3″, or let it flop into a no-mow carpet. A genuine step toward the natural approach short of full meadow.
candidates.curationNotes: Non-native cool-season turf, like tall fescue, but a meaningfully lower-input option. Seed from turf-seed specialists (no-mow / eco-lawn blends); not a native-nursery item.

candidates.name: Pennsylvania sedge
candidates.rationale: A native sedge that works as a no-mow lawn alternative in the shadier ground a fescue lawn struggles with — fine, soft, flopping to about six inches and spreading slowly into a green carpet under trees.
candidates.notes: The native answer for the shaded lawn edges, not the open sunny fairway — honestly, a sunny native turf-grass that takes regular mowing and foot traffic the way tall fescue does largely doesn't exist for the Southeast yet. Plant as plugs; needs little once established and tolerates light foot traffic.
candidates.curationNotes: Native, and the “don't limit our thinking” entry: a real native lawn alternative, scoped to where it actually works (shade), with the sunny-turf limitation stated plainly.

candidates.name: Cherry tree — a heritage planting
candidates.rationale: A cherry tree honoring the Kirschenbauer name — literally 'cherry farmer' in Bavaria. The site is what makes it feasible: at 2,873 ft, Fernwood sits in the Georgia mountains, one of the few parts of the state that actually meets a cherry's winter chill requirement (1,000–2,000 hours) — lowland Georgia can't, which is why cherries fail there. So this is a planting the elevation genuinely earns.
communityFit: Open, sunny, well-drained slope (full sun, good air movement)
Not a wet or low-lying spot
candidates.notes: WHAT WORKS HERE — Sour/tart cherry (Prunus cerasus) is the better bet, and the one that also matches the Bavarian heritage (Sauerkirsche / Morello are the classic Bavarian cherry, the Black-Forest-cake cherry). It's self-fertile (a single tree fruits — no pollinizer needed), hardier, and blooms a little later than sweet cherry so it dodges more spring frosts. UGA recommends 'Montmorency' and 'Early Richmond' for Georgia; a Morello leans most authentically Bavarian. WHAT'S HARDER — Sweet cherry (Prunus avium; e.g. 'Rainier') is possible at this elevation but tougher: it usually needs a second tree to pollinate, blooms earliest (most frost-exposed), and is the most disease-prone. THE CAVEATS EITHER WAY — the humid Southeast is hard on cherries: brown rot, cherry leaf spot (Montmorency is especially leaf-spot-prone), and powdery mildew all thrive in still, damp air, and early bloom means a late frost can take the crop. Site it in full sun on a breezy, well-drained spot and treat a good fruit year as a bonus, not a given. THE PICK we're circling: a sour/Morello cherry — it's both the most plantable choice for this site and the most Bavarian. The exact cultivar is Paul's to lock in (Montmorency = easiest to source + UGA-backed; a true Morello = most heritage-faithful).
candidates.curationNotes: Horticulture web-verified 2026-07-25 against UGA Extension 'Minor Fruits and Nuts in Georgia' (B992) + general SE cherry references: cherries need 1,000–2,000 chill hrs met only in GA's Piedmont/mountains; sour > sweet in GA; sour cherries self-fertile; humid-SE disease pressure (brown rot, leaf spot, powdery mildew) and early-bloom frost risk are the real limiters. Heritage tie (Kirschenbauer = cherry farmer, Bavaria) is Paul-stated. Intent, not yet planted.
